label: Statistical Inference and Differential Geometry
notes: Open the chapter. Here the geometry pays off: estimation theory acquires a coordinate-free shape. The deck follows printed pages 81 through 114 and connects estimators to geometry, recasts maximum likelihood as m-projection, derives the Cramer-Rao bound from the Fisher metric, and explains higher-order efficiency through the embedding curvature of the model.

label: Estimators and Geometry
notes: Frame an estimator as a map from samples to points on the model manifold. Unbiasedness, consistency, and efficiency all become geometric statements about how the estimator sits relative to the true distribution. The Fisher metric measures local error, and the dual connections describe how that error transports across the manifold during inference.

label: Maximum Likelihood as Projection
notes: Recast maximum-likelihood estimation as m-projection of the empirical distribution onto the model along a mixture geodesic. By the generalized Pythagorean theorem this projection minimizes the Kullback-Leibler divergence and is unique on a dually flat model. The geometric view makes the optimality of maximum likelihood transparent rather than computational.

label: Cramer-Rao Bound
notes: Derive the Cramer-Rao lower bound directly from the Fisher information metric: no unbiased estimator can have covariance smaller than the inverse Fisher matrix. Geometrically, the bound expresses that the metric sets the finest distinguishable scale on the model. Efficient estimators attain it, sitting exactly at the metric limit of precision.

label: Higher-Order Asymptotics
notes: Go beyond first order using curvature. The exponential and mixture curvatures of the model and of the estimator control second-order bias and variance. A model that is e-flat and an estimator that is m-flat achieve higher-order efficiency. Curvature thus quantifies exactly how much information is lost beyond the Cramer-Rao limit.

label: Recap
notes: Close the chapter. Estimators are maps into the model, maximum likelihood is m-projection, the Cramer-Rao bound is the Fisher metric limit, and curvature governs higher-order efficiency. Differential geometry turns asymptotic statistics into clean geometric statements, and Chapter 05 applies the same ideas to time series and linear systems.
